title: Locating Contact on Tendon-Driven Continuum Robots From Tendon Measurements Alone via Constrained Moving Horizon Estimation
authors: Haitham El-Hussieny
abstract: Tendon-driven continuum robots can reach through constrained spaces, but contact along their bodies is invisible to the sensors at their motors. We show that this is a structural limitation rather than a tuning problem: the map from contact forces to tendon measurements has a null space of dimension at least seven, so no estimator that leaves the contact support free can locate contact. When the obstacle geometry is known, however, non-penetration and complementarity make the contact force locally identifiable, and we prove that the resulting system with unknown contact inputs is locally exponentially strongly detectable. We present a constrained moving horizon estimator (MHE) that encodes these conditions and runs in real time as one quadratic program per sample, and we give a local, mode-wise robust stability result for it. In a finite- element benchmark of a two-section robot pressing and sliding on a wall, the estimator located contact to 0.9 mm and estimated contact force to 0.22 N, compared with 65 mm and 0.72 N for a tuned extended Kalman filter (EKF) with state projection. The estimator tolerated millimeter- level errors in the obstacle position and unmodeled wall friction, under which the projected EKF failed. Under randomized model mismatch over 40 trials, including unmodeled tendon friction, it remained better in force and location in every trial. Without contact, the MHE offered no advantage over the EKF, which confirms that its benefit comes from the contact constraints. This report extends a letter submitted to IEEE Control Systems Letters with complete proofs and additional experiments.

title: PhotoFinish: Portable Timerless Probing of Microarchitectural Latencies
authors: Tristan Hornetz, Eduard Ebert, Lorenz Hetterich, Lukas Gerlach, Michael Schwarz
abstract: Timing measurements are a fundamental building block of microarchitectural attacks, enabling software to convert otherwise invisible latency differences into architectural observations. Thus, restricting high-resolution timers is a common defense, especially in constrained environments such as web browsers. Timerless probing primitives provide an alternative approach. Instead of reading or constructing a timer, they observe architectural events that correlate with the microarchitectural state. However, such primitives typically rely on platform-specific behavior, and none generalizes across the wider computing landscape. In this paper, we present PhotoFinish, a portable timerless probing primitive that converts latency differences directly into an architectural value. PhotoFinish races an operation under test against a fixed reference in two parallel threads that then write unique values to the same shared location, resulting in a latency-dependent architectural value. PhotoFinish only requires parallel execution and shared memory, without constructing or reading a clock. We evaluate PhotoFinish on 38 CPUs spanning four ISAs and demonstrate reliable cache state classification across widely different microarchitectures, with comparable fidelity when compiled to WebAssembly and executed inside a browser. We further use PhotoFinish in AES T-table and Evict+Reload attacks, show that it applies beyond caches to TLB and execution-engine latencies, and demonstrate sufficient precision to identify the LLC slice of an address. Our results demonstrate shared-memory races as a generic and precise replacement for explicit timing, showing that restricting timers alone does not prevent software from observing fine-grained microarchitectural latency differences.

title: FlowMoP: Stochastic Multi-Person Motion Prediction
authors: Aadya Agrawal, Ho Kei Cheng, Alexander Schwing
abstract: Predicting the future motion of multiple people is inherently stochastic: the same observed history admits many plausible continuations depending on intent, coordination, and social context. Yet the dominant paradigm in multi-person 3D motion prediction remains deterministic, with existing methods producing a fixed number of outputs per agent. In contrast, we present a conditional flow matching framework that jointly generates diverse future motions for multiple agents, modeling both global trajectories and root-relative poses. A B-spline reparameterization compresses the generative state space while enforcing temporal smoothness, and a dual-stream transformer conditions each agent's predictions on observed neighbor motion for interaction-aware forecasting. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on CMU-Mocap (UMPM) and 3DPW, outperforming deterministic baselines on joint position error, pose error, and final displacement error despite producing a full predictive distribution. We additionally establish the first motion prediction baseline on WorldPose, a large-scale professional soccer dataset, where social conditioning demonstrably concentrates predictive uncertainty along interaction-constrained directions.
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 22 pages, including references and appendix

title: ZeoBench: A Benchmark for Self-Supervised Learning on 3D Zeolite Representations
authors: Aaron Sun, Yachan Liu, Ping Yang, Peng Bai, Subhransu Maji
abstract: Zeolites are an important class of porous crystalline materials with broad applications in gas storage, separations, and catalysis. Although hundreds of thousands of experimentally realized and hypothetical zeolite structures are known, identifying materials optimized for a target application remains challenging because property labels are expensive to obtain and available only for limited structure-molecule pairs. While prior work has demonstrated that 3D neural representations can predict zeolite properties effectively, it remains unclear which representation-learning strategies are most effective in the low-data regime relevant to materials discovery. We present ZeoBench, a benchmark for self-supervised learning on dense 3D representations of all-silica zeolites, and evaluate the resulting features on six existing downstream adsorption-property prediction tasks, across a range of training set sizes. Our study compares self-supervised 3D pretraining on volumetric zeolite data, adaptations of image-pretrained 2D ConvNets and vision transformers to 3D via multiview and channel-inflation strategies, and 3D ConvNets pretrained on out-of-domain volumetric datasets, alongside hand-crafted descriptors and supervised baselines. Using our pretraining and evaluation framework, we find self-supervised 3D representations outperform existing methods and achieve state-of-the-art performance across both in-domain label regimes and for the unseen domain of metal organic frameworks. Learned representations consistently outperform hand-crafted descriptors, and convolutional architectures are generally more effective than vision transformers in this setting. These results establish ZeoBench as a practical benchmark for 3D representation learning in zeolites and provide guidance for data-limited adsorption property prediction.

title: Scenario Orchestration for Closed-loop Policy Evaluation of Autonomous Driving
authors: Frieda Rong, Zhaoyue Wang, Veer Kapadia, Vishaka Rajani, Aren A. Babikian, Xujie Si, Mahsa Golchoubian, Raquel Urtasun, Igor Gilitschenski
abstract: Scenario-based simulation is central to evaluating autonomous-driving policies, but a scenario scripted before execution (i.e., with predetermined, fixed actor routes and speeds) may not preserve its intended interaction once the tested ego policy responds in closed loop. Scripted scenarios cannot adapt to unanticipated ego behavior, while learned traffic actors may remain reactive without reliably realizing a particular scenario intent. We introduce a scenario orchestrator that continuously monitors the joint traffic state and adapts non-ego actors through re-timing, re-routing, and role reassignment for creating a specific scenario intent. At each step, the orchestrator solves a constrained optimization problem that preserves the intended interaction while limiting interventions and maintaining traffic feasibility. We further distinguish scenario realization from policy failure, allowing a test to first be judged based on whether the intended interaction occurred and then by how the ego policy responded. Experiments in the CARLA simulator across multiple scenario families and driving policies show that orchestration realizes targeted interactions more reliably than scripted and learned actor-level baselines, particularly under variations in initial conditions and ego behavior. These results support closed-loop scenario orchestration as a tool for controlled and reproducible policy evaluation.

title: On the (non-)closedness of the set of ReLU networks
authors: Eloi Martinet, Leon Bungert
abstract: We prove that the set $\mathcal{N}_N$ of ReLU networks with one hidden layer and at most $N\in\mathbb N$ neurons is weakly closed in $W^{1,p}(Ω)$, for a bounded connected open set $Ω\subset\mathbb R^d$. Consequently, every coercive, weakly lower semicontinuous energy on this space attains its minimum over $\mathcal{N}_N$. This covers the Deep Ritz method with convex integrands, Sobolev training and Lipschitz learning. Moreover, as the weight decay parameter tends to zero, minimizers of the regularized problem converge, up to subsequences, to minimizers with minimal parameter norm. We also prove that the set of ReLU networks with two hidden layers of bounded widths is not closed in $W^{1,p}(Ω)$ or in $C(\overlineΩ)$. This disproves a conjecture of Petersen, Raslan and Voigtlaender.

title: CPU-ARC: Agentic Reasoning Caching for on-CPU Reasoning Reuse
authors: Peter Belcak, Greg Heinrich, Saurav Muralidharan, Shizhe Diao, Pavlo Molchanov
abstract: Large language models reinvent the wheel all the time. They conflate task-solving with the execution of the solutions, which forces them to solve every problem from scratch. We show that once a task has been reasoned through, the application of its solution to a new problem instance can be done very efficiently and with little involvement from language models. We introduce agentic reasoning caching, a method for constructing robust CPU-executable agentic reasoning caches (ARCs) from LLM reasoning traces. ARCs show on-par performance with frontier LLMs across a range of difficult mathematical and scientific tasks, are fully explainable, continually trainable, robust to input perturbations, and 16-291x cheaper to invoke than the source model.

title: SciCheck: A Framework for Verifying the Integrity of Deep Learning Training
authors: Alexander Nguyen, Dylan Gresham, Gaby G. Dagher, Min Long
abstract: Deep learning training is difficult to verify within a scientific workflow: its architecture, hyperparameters, and procedure are rarely fixed until training has been attempted, and two honest runs never produce the same weights, so recomputation cannot serve as a check. We present SciCheck, a framework in which the scientist explores training configurations freely and posts a blueprint to a provenance ledger for each candidate they want verified, and a verifying scientist judges the resulting run in two layers: a statistical judge model that compares per-step gradient statistics against the verifier's own reference run, and a spot-check that re-executes randomly chosen training segments whose checkpoints are committed to the ledger one epoch at a time. On an MLP, a CNN, and an autoencoder at 100k-500k parameters, under gradient sign flipping, label poisoning, and fabricated runs, SciCheck reaches F1 of 0.966, 0.906, and 0.976 while rejecting 0-4.4% of honest runs. For the attacks we test, the spot-check accounts for most of this accuracy, and we characterize what each layer can detect. The effective-signal statistic falls as $(1-2s)^2$ under a sign flip of severity $s$, so gradient statistics alone catch strong enough sign flips, while fabricated runs that replay genuine statistics look no more anomalous than honest runs to any statistical detector we test. The spot-check catches fully fabricated segments with probability at least $1-(1-s)^k$ for $k$ sampled segments when the draws stay hidden until the run is committed, which roughly matches our measurements and lets a verifier choose $k$ for a target soundness. Verification costs 1.5-2.3x one retraining, mostly for the verifier's reference run; each submission's spot-check takes under 1.5 s, and per-epoch commitments reduce checkpoint storage 5-17x compared with keeping every checkpoint.

title: Video-Coder: Reinforcing Agentic Coding for Video Generation
authors: Chaoyang Wang, Sicheng Gao, Junan Hu, Kunyang Li, Dongyang Chen, Yiyang Zhou, Huaxiu Yao, Yong Jae Lee, Radu Timofte, Yuzhang Shang
abstract: Recent years have witnessed remarkable progress in video generation in terms of visual quality and temporal consistency. However, generating videos with precise spatial structure, coherent motion dynamics, and controllable scene composition remains challenging. In this paper, we introduce Video-Coder, the first attempt to train a code-driven video generation agent, which autonomously writes and executes code to construct a dynamic 3D scene (Draft Video) that provides structure and motion signals to downstream video generators. To support this paradigm, we design a dedicated data pipeline and curate two high-quality datasets, Video-Coder-SFT-6k and Video-Coder-RL-2k, which contain diverse prompts and ground-truth reference videos. We further develop the Video- Coder Harness, a unified interactive environment integrating code execution, 3D scene rendering, and execution feedback for agent training and inference. We then train Video-Coder with SFT fol- lowed by harness-native agentic reinforcement learning with dual reward feedback, which combines execution-based and video-based rewards. Additionally, we design an annealing training strategy that gradually reduces the execution reward over time, allowing the model to rely more on the video reward in the later training stages. Experiments show that Video-Coder achieves significant gains, improving Minimax-H3 by approximately 7 points on PhyGenBench and 24 points on VBench-2.0. We hope this work can serve as an open foundation for coding agents in video generation, and we fully open-source our data, models, and code

title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
authors: Chen Chen, Omid Bagherieh, Naveen Nikamanth Appiah Balaji, Jesse T. Gonzalez, Negin Heravi, Fahad Islam, Xueting Li, Jean-Baptiste Regli, Kejia Ren, Petr Švec, David J. Yoon, Matthias Müller, Vladlen Koltun
abstract: Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.

title: Electoral Intelligence: A Neural Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial Model for Forecasting Swedish Municipal Elections
authors: Haodong Qi, Stefano M. Iacus, Pieter Bevelander, Derek S. Hutcheson
abstract: Forecasting local elections is difficult because electoral competition is geographically heterogeneous, highly overdispersed, and characterized by many party-municipality combinations with little or no electoral activity. This article develops a bounded neural zero-inflated negative binomial (ZINB) model for forecasting party-level vote counts in Swedish municipal elections. The model combines a count component for expected votes, a zero-inflation component for structural electoral absence, municipality-specific dispersion, and learned embeddings capturing latent party, municipality, and party-municipality structure. Model training relies on data from the 2014, 2018, and 2022 Swedish municipal elections and performance is evaluated on a held-out set of municipalities. Testing results show strong predictive accuracy in both vote counts and vote shares. Explanatory diagnostics indicate that latent party structure, local party-municipality relationships, electoral persistence, organizational capacity, and candidate-electorate representational similarity are among the most important determinants of predictive performance. Following model evaluation and diagnostics, the selected specification is refit on all historical data and applied to generate forecasts for the 2026 municipal elections. The proposed framework provides a flexible approach for studying local electoral competition in multiparty systems characterized by heterogeneous party presence and substantial geographic variation.

title: Deep-Learning Algorithm for Indeterminate Thyroid Nodules: Comparison and Combination with Molecular Testing
authors: Jichen Yang, Jeffrey Ashton, Jikai Zhang, Maciej A. Mazurowski, Benjamin Wildman-Tobriner
abstract: Thyroid nodules with indeterminate cytology (Bethesda III) carry an intermediate risk of malignancy, and molecular testing is widely used to decide between surgery and surveillance, but it is costly and not universally available. We investigated whether a convolutional neural network (CNN) applied to routine ultrasound images can stratify Bethesda III nodules, and how it compares and combines with molecular testing. We retrospectively identified 466 nodule records from 418 patients who underwent molecular testing (Afirma or ThyroSeq). A CNN pre-trained on determinate nodules was adapted to indeterminate nodules with soft labels and transfer learning. After removal of duplicate records, 119 nodules with surgical pathology were used for development and 47 were held out for testing. On the test set, the deep learning (DL) model achieved an AUC of 0.73 (95% CI 0.51-0.94), compared with 0.55 (0.38-0.71) for molecular testing (P = 0.15). At a cut-off inherited from the original algorithm, the DL model was more specific than molecular testing (0.95 vs 0.32; P < 0.001), with a higher positive predictive value (0.67 vs 0.21), a lower sensitivity (0.44 vs 0.78; P = 0.25) and a similar negative predictive value (0.88 vs 0.86). All six DL-positive test nodules were molecular-positive, and the DL output split the molecular-positive nodules into a high-risk (4/6 malignant) and a lower-risk group (3/27 malignant; P = 0.01). Surgical verification was strongly driven by the molecular result (99% of positive vs 19% of negative results), and molecular-test accuracy depended on the platform. A logistic regression of the DL output, nodule size and the molecular result dropped the DL term and did not improve on the DL output alone. Ultrasound DL complemented molecular testing for Bethesda III nodules, in particular by identifying molecular-positive nodules at lower risk of malignancy.

title: Drift-admissibility via Optimal Transport
authors: Abigail Langbridge, Enrico Biffis, Jakub Mareček, Robert Shorten
abstract: We introduce structure-aware optimal transport diagnostics for assessing whether empirical time-series dynamics are compatible with a prescribed predictable-drift class. Our approach translates a pathwise property of stochastic processes into a finite-dimensional projection problem over empirical transition laws, encoding admissibility as row-wise moment constraints on local couplings and quantifying deviations via a Kullback--Leibler projection gap $G_{λ,k}$. This yields both a principled diagnostic and a scalable Bregman--Dykstra algorithm that retains the efficiency of Sinkhorn-type methods while incorporating structural constraints. Calibrated against a Brownian reference null, $G_{λ,k}$ separates process classes that are indistinguishable by second-order statistics alone---including fractional Brownian motion and BSS processes sharing identical Hurst indices---without asymptotic resampling or continuous-time recovery. This positions the method as a general tool for structure-aware model validation of sequential data.

title: Online and Survey Representations of Well-Being: Coherence and Cross-Source Correspondence
authors: Stefano M. Iacus, Giuseppe Porro, Haodong Qi
abstract: Digital traces may complement population surveys in the measurement of well-being, but the two sources do not necessarily capture identical constructs. We compare the Human Flourishing Geographic Index (HFGI) with World Values Survey and European Social Survey measures across three domains using structural equation models. The results show strong within-source coherence and construct-specific cross-source correspondence. Cross-source convergence varies across domains; the observed pattern is consistent with stronger correspondence where the underlying indicators are more closely aligned conceptually. Near-perfect agreement would be unexpected, since surveys elicit standardized self-reports, whereas HFGI captures naturally occurring public expressions. HFGI should therefore be viewed as a distinct but empirically connected measurement system that complements survey-based evidence on well-being.

title: Structure is in the zoom: probing neural symmetry through dimensionality scaling
authors: Adil Amin
abstract:
How much of a neural population's measured dimensionality is the code, and how much is the act of measuring it? The slope of the participation ratio against subsample size is reported for cortical populations and for the layers of language models as a number that belongs to the system. It does not. One patch of eleven thousand mouse V1 neurons returns three slopes, 0.25 along random stimulus subsets, 0.31 along drift direction, 0.35 along neuron count, and only the middle one carries structure; the other two are the sampling floor.
  We split every exponent into that floor and a shift earned along a declared axis, and read the shift against two nulls: permuting the labels, and permuting them only among samples that share a nuisance. On V1 the direction-aligned shift clears the label null in eight of eight grating recordings, is positive in 32 of 32 animals in a second laboratory, and reads both sectors of the code's O(2) symmetry. The even sector sets how the ladder starts: it decides which order of adding classes climbs faster, predicts the opposite order in an equivariant network, and flows under coarse-graining by a closed-form factor that says what orientation columns do to mesoscale signals. The odd sector, carried by the direction-selective neurons, keeps the ladder climbing past half the classes. On language models the same split separates content inherited from the tokens from construction built with depth, on five architectures, and the second null shows that a grammaticality signal of twenty standard deviations is entirely carrier composition. With a floor and a declared axis, dimensionality scaling is an axis-resolved measurement, and where the axis follows a known symmetry it resolves the sector content of the code. The instrument, rung, trains no probe and reads any array or any Hugging Face model layer by layer (https://github.com/adilamin89/structure-in-the-zoom).
comment: 63 pages, 20 figures. Code, data and the rung tool: https://github.com/adilamin89/structure-in-the-zoom

title: pESTO: Iterative p-greedy kernel regression with risk-driven Early STOpping
authors: L. Bruni Bruno, P. Massa, E. Perracchione, M. Trombini
abstract: Kernel-based greedy algorithms select suitable approximation nodes by minimizing point-wise error indicators, such as the power function; in this context, they are usually referred to as p-greedy approaches. In the presence of noisy data, deterministic criteria may fail, as the discrepancy between the true solution and its estimate is influenced by both approximation error and noise amplification, and the balance between the two is unknown. This study explicitly separates these two contributions, which are governed by the power function and a Lebesgue-type term, respectively. These bounds motivate the use of the Stein's unbiased risk estimator (SURE) as a proxy of the mean squared error, which in turn provides a principled and computable stopping criterion for the number of nodes to select in the p-greedy procedure. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this approach effectively balances deterministic accuracy and statistical noise contributions.

title: ELPAC: Endpoint-Anchored Latent Progression with Stage-Varying Multimodal Coordination
authors: Shengxian Ding, Yifei Zhang, Xinyuan Tian, Yuanshuang Guo, Yize Zhao
abstract: Aging cohorts increasingly combine imaging, plasma, and cognitive measurements, but most subjects provide only a partially observed cross-sectional snapshot, leaving latent stage, progression subtype, and stage-varying multimodal coordination to be inferred jointly. Existing methods estimate the cohort-level aging process, model covariance under observed covariates, or fuse modalities for prediction. However, they rarely target the joint problem of endpoint-anchored staging and progression-resolved residual coordination across modalities, even though subject staging, subtype assignment, and multimodal interplay are mutually dependent. We introduce ELPAC, a Bayesian framework with two interlocking constructions. The first integrates subtype trajectories backward from clinically reliable endpoint groups along biologically structured velocity components encoding modality-specific monotone direction and optional sequential ordering priors. The second factorizes residual multimodal variation around the inferred stage axis into sparse coordination axes whose loadings and activations expose which multimodal patterns are operative in each subtype and when they emerge, with stage-resolved variation supplying the auxiliary structure for conditional identifiability. We use a scalable amortized variational inference scheme that enables joint posterior inference at cohort scale with single-pass deployment on new subjects. On synthetic data and a harmonized ADNI+NACC/SCAN Alzheimer's cohort, ELPAC demonstrates accurate latent-structure recovery, well-calibrated prediction intervals, and biologically interpretable multimodal coordination programs that differ by subtype.

title: GenStrain: Multi-Conditional Generative Diffusion Model To Synthesize High-quality Motion and Strain Maps From Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Images
authors: Rishov Paul, Sona Ghadimi, Cristiane C. Singulane, Amit R. Patel, Frederick H. Epstein, Miaomiao Zhang
abstract: This paper presents GenStrain, a novel method for synthesizing high-quality cardiac motion-based strain maps from routinely collected cine cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) images. Existing approaches typically rely on image registration to estimate motion (a sequence of displacements) from cine CMR images, but cine CMR presents very sparse trackable intramyocardial features, presenting challenges to estimate intramyocardial motion. An advanced imaging technique, Displacement Encoding with Stimulated Echoes (DENSE) CMR, is considered as the gold standard for strain assessment, but it requires additional acquisitions, which are not ideal for efficient clinical workflows. To address this gap, we introduce GenStrain, a novel framework designed to learn the data distribution of highly accurate cardiac motion captured by DENSE. In particular, we develop a diffusion process in motion space, where spatiotemporal continuity is carefully considered. To fully leverage both cine CMR images and their associated motion patterns, we introduce a multi-conditional conditioning strategy that integrates anatomical features and motion representations learned by a spatiotemporal registration model to guide the generation process. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed model, GenStrain, outperforms existing strain analysis methods based on displacement estimates from both traditional registration approaches and state-of-the-art (SOTA) deep learning models. Our model represents a promising step toward more accurate cardiac function assessment and holds great potential for clinical translation. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Rishov-MIA/GenStrain.

title: Spiking neuromodulation: a linear control perspective
authors: Fulvio Forni, Rodolphe Sepulchre
abstract: Neuronal excitability is a nonlinear phenomenon, and the complexity of spiking experimental traces sometimes looks defeating. The present paper takes the view point that excitability is a neuromodulated property, and aims to demonstrate that the neuromodulation of spiking is amenable to the classical linear analysis tools of control theory. We illustrate the value of linear feedback analysis as an alternative to bifurcation analysis in the simple yet classical example of spiking modulation by the A-type potassium current.
comment: 8 pages. Submitted to European Control Conference ECC 2027

title: Just CaloCHILL: fast hadronic shower generation in a learned latent space
authors: Henry Day-Hall, Frank Gaede, Gregor Kasieczka, Katja Krüger, Martina Mozzanica
abstract: Calorimeter showers are the most expensive part of detector simulation, and highly granular calorimeters, in which a single hadronic shower leaves thousands of energy deposits, make them more expensive still. We present CaloCHILL (Calorimeter Hits In Learned Latents), a generative model that does not produce these deposits one by one: instead it generates a compact summary of the shower in a learned latent space and expands it to full resolution only at the end. The complete shower, including the arrival time of every hit, is built in three stages: a flow-matching model first sets the number of hits and the earliest hit time in each calorimeter layer, a mean-flow model then generates the latent summary, and the decompressor of a variational autoencoder turns it into the full point cloud, giving every hit its position, energy and time. Sparse attention along the shower axis keeps this compression affordable for showers with thousands of hits. On positive-pion showers in the calorimeter of the International Large Detector, a proposed detector for the FCC-ee, CaloCHILL reproduces the main shower observables, including their time structure. This new model is 600 times faster than its predecessor, while improving on all accuracy metrics considered.
comment: 25 pages, 19 figures, 11 tables. Code: https://github.com/FLC-QU-hep/CaloCHILL, data: https://doi.org/10.25592/uhhfdm.22077

title: Personalized health coaching via coachable health age and counterfactual wearable trajectories
authors: Simon A. Lee, Zeinab Esmaeilpour, Menglian Zhou, Marius Guerard, Sohrab Sidhu, Alexandru Solot, Hamid Palangi, Pramod Rudrapatna, Ming-Zher Poh, Max A. Xu, Daniel McDuff, Dimitrios Antos, Yuzhe Yang, Jeffrey N. Chiang, Anthony Z. Faranesh, Lindsey Sunden, Mark Malhotra, Shwetak Patel, A. Ali Heydari, Ahmed A. Metwally
abstract: Personalized health coaching requires moving beyond retrospective wearable summaries toward quantitative, actionable behavioral prescriptions. We introduce Coachable Health Age (CHA), an interpretable health-age metric built from modifiable physiological and behavioral signals passively captured by consumer wearables. Across the WEAR-ME (N=2,780), All of Us (N=22,748), and longitudinal Fitbit (N=1,464) cohorts, CHA aligns with established cardiometabolic health constructs and improves prognostic discrimination for incident cardiovascular and metabolic disease beyond age, sex, and body mass index. To enable prospective behavioral optimization, we developed Sensor World Model (SensorWM), an action-conditioned wearable world model pretrained on over 2.2 million person-weeks of longitudinal sensor data from approximately 100,000 participants. SensorWM accurately forecasts multi-week physiological responses to candidate lifestyle changes ($R^2=0.664$), outperforming generic time-series foundation models while preserving downstream clinical signal for diabetes, hypertension, and other health outcomes. Finally, we integrate CHA and SensorWM into an agentic counterfactual coaching system to synthesize personalized 12-week coaching plans. In blinded paired reviews, certified lifestyle coaches preferred counterfactual-grounded plans over plans grounded in wearable history alone for overall quality (71.4%, P < 0.001) and anticipated adherence (71.0%, P < 0.001), and board-certified clinicians judged 99.2% of counterfactual-grounded plans to meet clinical safety criteria (vs. 97.6% of comparison plans). Automated evaluations across the full cohort (N=2,780) also favored counterfactual-grounded plans. By closing the loop between longitudinal tracking, trajectory prediction, and counterfactual coaching, our framework provides a scalable path to systematically improve cardiometabolic health.

title: Evasive subspaces, minimal rank-metric codes and subspace designs via auxiliary fields
authors: Alessandro Giannoni
abstract: We extend the auxiliary-field method for scattered subspaces to evasive subspaces and subspace designs. For $1\le h\le k<hn$ and coprime $h,k+1$ with $n(k-h+1)\ge k+1$, we construct spanning $(h,k)$-evasive $\mathbb{F}_q$-subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_{q^n}^r$ of dimension $rn(k-h+1)/(k+1)$ in every sufficiently large admissible ambient dimension, with a threshold independent of $q$. When $k<n$, this dimension is maximum. The proof combines an intersection lemma, a rank-support density inequality, scalar orbit counting, and a profile preserved by direct sums. The coding consequences include, for every fixed odd extension degree $m\ge3$ and every sufficiently large $K$, minimal rank-metric codes of optimal length $2K$ with first two generalized weights $(m+1)/2$ and $m+1$. For these codes the stable profile is equivalent to minimality with the largest possible minimum distance; for even $m$ the analogous class consists of minimal MRD codes. More generally, for $1\leτ\le m-2$ and $\gcd(m,τ+1)=1$, we obtain nondegenerate $τ$-minimal codes of length $(τ+1)K$ for every sufficiently large $K$, uniformly in $q$. We also construct maximum $h$-designs whose number of members grows exponentially with the ambient dimension at fixed $q,n,h$, and the associated maximum sum-rank distance (MSRD) codes with a growing number of equal long blocks. In extension degree five, the ordinary and $2$-minimal constructions hold for every $q$ and every $K\ge32$ and $K\ge59$, respectively.

title: Vector Lyapunov functions for nonconvex constrained optimization
authors: Torbjørn Cunis, Ilya Kolmanovsky
abstract: Nonconvex constrained optimization problems are commonly solved by a Newton method for necessary conditions (sequential linear/quadratic programming) or a barrier reformulation (interior-point methods). We present a vector Lyapunov analysis for Newton-type algorithms based on constraint violation and optimality of the primal solutions to a sequence of approximate optimization problems. We thus prove local stability and convergence by constructing a strict Lyapunov function for the primal solution.
comment: Extended version of submission to the 2027 European Control Conference

title: Branch-Extended Automatic Differentiation
authors: Jan Hückelheim, Jeffrey Larson, Matt Menickelly
abstract: We present branch-extended automatic differentiation (BEAD), a software package that provides information about inactive branches of piecewise-differentiable functions, intended for use in nonsmooth optimization algorithms. BEAD is implemented in Python, building on the popular JAX framework. For supported nonsmooth operations such as abs and max, BEAD identifies alternative branches within tolerance from the given input, and computes gradients of the resulting branches extended to the given input. Such information has been previously used for robust optimization methods, but has required error-prone and tedious manual differentiation, unlike BEAD, which is fully automated for functions written in NumPy-like JAX code. Our experiments show that our approach is as accurate as manually written derivative code, and offers more flexibility in modifying the function and choosing between branch-discovery rules. While we were originally motivated by the manifold sampling algorithm for nonsmooth composite objectives, we also integrate BEAD branch-extension gradients into a nonsmooth BFGS-SQP solver. On two small nonsmooth test problems, the resulting path-aware search resolves failures or substantially reduces the number of evaluations required by the BFGS-SQP solver.

title: Compressed Per-Player Local Methods for Multiplayer Federated Learning: Exact Convergence via Increment Sharing
authors: Bhavika Balani, TaeHo Yoon, Nicolas Loizou
abstract: Multiplayer Federated Learning (MpFL), introduced by Yoon et al. (2025), extends classical federated learning to settings where clients are rational players in a game with individual objectives and strategies, seeking an equilibrium. A natural baseline is Per-Player Local SGD (PEARL-SGD), where each player performs several local SGD steps before exchanging strategies through a central server. However, the original PEARL-SGD formulation does not extend cleanly to compressed communication. Directly compressing the players' strategies can prevent convergence to the equilibrium, even with deterministic gradients. To address this issue, we reformulate PEARL-SGD so that players communicate local strategy increments rather than the strategies themselves. Without compression, the two formulations are equivalent, but with compression, increment sharing preserves exact convergence, allowing us to design the communication-efficient compressed PEARL-SGD (C-PEARL-SGD). Beyond compression, we also consider variance reduction as another axis of improvement, introducing PEARL-SVRG and its compressed variant C-PEARL-SVRG. Under the original MpFL assumptions, we establish convergence guarantees for all variants through a unified parametric inequality. Numerical experiments, including distributed spectrum sensing, demonstrate the practical benefits of our methods over vanilla PEARL-SGD.

title: A Gamma-Mixture Solution for Definite Noncentral Complex Gaussian Quadratic Forms
authors: Fernando D. Almeida García, Carlos R. Nogueira da Silva, Felipe A. P. de Figueiredo, Rausley A. A. de Souza, Michel Daoud Yacoub, José Cândido Silveira Santos Filho
abstract: Finding exact solutions for the statistics of definite noncentral complex Gaussian quadratic forms (CGQFs) has long been a challenging problem. Among existing exact approaches, Raphaeli's formulation [1] remains the most computationally efficient. However, its analytical tractability is hindered by the dependence of its series coefficients on the evaluation variable, which confines their statistics to the probability density function (PDF) and cumulative distribution function (CDF). This paper overcomes this limitation by deriving novel Gamma-mixture representations for the PDF and CDF of positive- and negative-definite noncentral CGQFs. The resulting structure broadens Raphaeli's statistical framework beyond the PDF and CDF to a wider class of CGQF functionals and a substantial range of practical applications. In particular, expectations of integrable functions of definite noncentral CGQFs are expressed as weighted sums of the corresponding expectations over Gamma random variables, enabling the direct derivation of moments, transforms, and performance measures. Moreover, the proposed formulation reduces the single-point complexity from \(O\!\left(n^2K+nK^2\right)\) for Raphaeli's method to \(O\!\left(nK+K^2\right)\), where \(n\) denotes the quadratic-form dimension and \(K\) the truncation order. The proposed Gamma-mixture structure also enables closed-form approximations that, by construction, remain valid probability distributions for any truncation order. In addition, uniform PDF and CDF truncation-error bounds are derived, allowing prescribed-accuracy truncation. As a sample application, we derive the first reported exact average bit error rate expression for maximal-ratio combining receivers with an arbitrary number of branches under an arbitrary positive-definite Rician correlation structure.

title: Measurement-Aware Multimodal LLM for No-Reference Low-Dose CT Quality Assessment
authors: Kerem Basim, Tolga Demiroglu, Mehmet Ozan Unal, Metin Ertas, Isa Yildirim
abstract: No-reference image quality assessment (IQA) of low-dose CT predicts the score that radiologists would assign to a slice without a full-dose reference, as needed to compare dose protocols and denoisers. Trained CT IQA networks agree well with radiologists but output only a score, whereas multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can explain a score but perform poorly on CT when only prompted. We propose a measurement-aware MLLM, built on Qwen3.8-27B, that rates a slice from its image together with six image-domain measurements of noise, sharpness, high-frequency content and streaks, given to the language model as percentiles in text. On the LDCT-IQA 2023 test set, it reaches an Overall score of 2.735, on par with the retrained challenge winner (2.735) and MedSigLIP-FiLM (2.713), and substantially above its base MLLM used as a zero-shot agent. Shuffling the measurements at test time reduces the score by 0.048, mostly through noise, but the same measurements also lead the model to assign higher scores to over-smoothed denoised images.
comment: 5 pages, 2 figures, 3 tables. Submitted to IEEE ISBI 2027

title: Multi-Model Over-the-Air Federated Learning via Transceiver Beamforming and Device Grouping
authors: Chong Zhang, Min Dong, Ben Liang, Ali Afana, Yahia A. Eldemerdash Ahmed
abstract: This paper considers uplink communication design for training multiple independent machine learning models via wireless federated learning. To reduce communication delay, we utilize multi-antenna beamforming and propose a multi-model over-the-air (M-OTA) uplink transmission and aggregation method for simultaneous training of multiple models. Devices are formed into groups for local model training based on the model assignments per communication round and simultaneously perform OTA aggregation over a multi-access channel. Based on the M-OTA transmission and reception process, we formulate a joint optimization of transmit and receive beamforming and device grouping over $T$ communication rounds to maximize the training convergence rates of all models. We analyze the per-model optimality gap, which captures the impact of noisy aggregation and inter-model interference on the learning performance. We further show that the $T$-round joint optimization problem can be decomposed into per-round online optimization to devise solutions. Following this, we propose a device grouping strategy that explores channel correlation among devices to maximize OTA aggregation performance. Furthermore, we present a low-complexity iterative algorithm for joint transmit-receive beamforming with closed-form updates. Simulation shows that our proposed M-OTA approach substantially outperforms the conventional single-model sequential OTA approach and other commonly used beamforming schemes.
comment: 16 pages, 6 figures. Accepted by IEEE Transactions on Wireless Communications, 2026

title: Blind Noise Equalization for Large Data Matrices under General Variance Profiles
authors: Boris Landa, Francesco Strino, Fabio Parisi, Ruiqi Li, Yuval Kluger
abstract: Low-rank approximation is a basic tool for inference from large and noisy data matrices. However, when noise variances differ across entries, a setting known as heteroskedasticity, the noise can distort the observed spectrum, producing spurious components and obscuring weak signals. To address these challenges, we develop BRINE (Blind Resolvent-based Iterative Noise Equalizer), a data-driven procedure that iteratively rescales rows and columns to equalize the average noise variance across both dimensions. Under suitable conditions, this procedure restores the Marchenko-Pastur law for the noise spectrum and can amplify signal components without prior knowledge of the signal or noise structure. A key idea underlying our approach is to equalize the diagonal entries of the data resolvent as a proxy for equalizing the unknown noise variances. At the population level, we identify a potential function that characterizes this equalization and motivates an iterative minimization procedure. We prove convergence of the iterations to the true equalizer for arbitrary positive variance profiles, with a geometric rate under mild conditions. The updates can be estimated directly from noisy data, and we establish probabilistic error bounds for the scaling factors. Simulations and experiments across diverse biological data modalities and preprocessing pipelines illustrate the effectiveness of our approach.

title: High-Dimensional Off-Policy Evaluation without Sample Splitting using an Onsager Correction
authors: Saksham Jain, Guillaume Braun, Masaaki Imaizumi
abstract: Reward models used for off-policy evaluation (OPE) are commonly selected using held-out data. When sample size and context dimension grow proportionally, the difference in test risk between models fitted on the full sample and on a fixed fraction of it need not vanish. Held-out evaluation can therefore consistently estimate the test risk of the model trained on the smaller sample, but because the relative ranking of candidate reward models can change after full-data refitting, held-out selection can be suboptimal. We develop an Onsager-corrected, target-policy-weighted criterion that estimates the full-data reward model's out-of-sample risk under the target policy using only its training observations. This enables early stopping along the full-data gradient-descent trajectory without sample splitting. For neural networks with fixed depth and hidden width under Gaussian contexts, single-index rewards, context-dependent multi-index target policies, and known context-independent logging, we prove uniform consistency of our criterion over a fixed finite set of gradient-descent iterates and a near-oracle guarantee for the selected reward model. The same correction yields a doubly robust estimator that consistently estimates the true policy value without sample splitting, even when reward-model prediction error does not vanish. Experiments show decreasing risk-estimation error as dimension grows at a fixed sample-to-dimension ratio, and improved reward-model selection relative to held-out baselines. Empirically, our correction also reduces the root mean squared error of doubly robust value estimates computed from the same data used to fit and select the reward models.

title: An Ultra-Low-Noise Tunable TIA in 45nm Silicon Photonics for Electro-Optical Ultrasound Data Acquisition
authors: Marziyeh Rezaei, Sridhar Singhal, Alp A. Derin, Soner Sonmezoglu, Sajjad Moazeni
abstract: This paper presents the design and experimental characterization of a 32-channel, WDM-compatible electronic-photonic receiver array fabricated in the GlobalFoundries 45nm monolithic silicon photonics process. Optimized for miniaturized, millimeter-scale electro-optical ultrasound data acquisition probes for broadband photo-acoustic imaging (PAI), the chip utilizes integrated micro-ring resonator (MRR) demultiplexers and photodiode (PD) arrays to decode multi-wavelength acoustic signals outside the body. This work focuses specifically on the comprehensive characterization of the receiver front-end, evaluating both the optical WDM filter bank and the transimpedance amplifier (TIA) performance. Monolithic co-integration minimizes critical photodiode-to-TIA interface parasitics. The TIA incorporates a DC-offset cancellation loop that compensates for photodiode-induced offset currents while providing tunable low-frequency cutoff control over a range of 30 kHz to 1.5 MHz. This tunability enables effective suppression of flicker noise and improves overall signal integrity. The front-end achieves the peak transimpedance gain of 144 dB$Ω$ while maintaining an ultra-low input-referred noise current density of $1\text{ pA}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$, demonstrating a highly scalable architecture for high-sensitivity intravascular and endobronchial imaging.

title: Beyond the Lower-Star Filtration: Alternative Filtration Methods for Persistent Homology
authors: Innocent Abaa, Umar Islambekov
abstract: In the lower-star filtration (LSF), simplices are assigned filtration values according to the maximum-vertex rule, with each simplex entering the filtration when its highest-valued vertex appears. A limitation of this construction is that some higher-dimensional simplices may enter simultaneously with their boundary faces, causing certain topological features to be filled immediately upon formation and thus not appear in the resulting persistence diagram. To address this limitation, we propose three alternative filtration methods: the \(\varepsilon\)-lower-star filtration (ELSF), the \(L_p\) filtration (LpF), and the softmax filtration (SMF). {ELSF introduces a dimension-dependent delay to the maximum-vertex rule,} allowing higher-dimensional simplices to enter the filtration after their boundary faces, whereas {LpF and SMF use aggregation functions that depend on all vertex values rather} than solely on their maximum. By modifying how filtration values are assigned, these methods allow simplices to enter the filtration more progressively, so that topological features such as loops and voids may persist over longer filtration intervals rather than being filled immediately. Consequently, the resulting persistence diagrams may include persistence features that are not observed under LSF, potentially providing useful information for distinguishing data populations. Experimental results on simulated and real-world datasets demonstrate that the proposed filtration methods are computationally efficient and can provide greater sensitivity to structural differences in the data than LSF.
comment: This is the published version of the article. Published in *International Journal of Topology*, MDPI, DOI: 10.3390/ijt3040025. Link to the official version: https://doi.org/10.3390/ijt3040025

title: FoundaRF: A Physics-Informed Foundation Model Framework for Radio-Frequency Passive Components
authors: Houbo He, Chris Han, Hyunsu Chae, Lei Xia, Qiang Zhou, Lawrence Liu, Sensen Li, David Z. Pan, Taiyun Chi
abstract: Designing RF/mmWave passive components is a time-consuming process that relies heavily on expert knowledge and iterative EM simulations. Although recent ML surrogate models have shown great promise in accelerating passive design, they remain task-specific and lack generalization. This paper presents FoundaRF, a foundation model framework that unifies passive layout modeling across diverse layout structures and technologies. It combines a self-supervised encoder with adaptive layout processing and physics-aware decoders to enable few-shot transfer. Experiments across four semiconductor technologies show strong generalization to unseen structures, outperforming baselines with up to a 3.3x reduction in prediction error, reducing labeled-data requirements by up to fourfold, and substantially shortening design turnaround. FoundaRF establishes a scalable and data-efficient solution for RF/mmWave passive design automation.
comment: Accepted for publication in the proceedings of the 2026 IEEE/ACM International Conference on Computer-Aided Design (ICCAD 2026)

title: Capacity of Multi-Layer Manhattan-Grid UAV Corridors Served by Terrestrial 5G NR Networks
authors: Saad Masrur, M M Sadman Shafi, Md Sharif Hossen, Ismail Guvenc
abstract: Advanced air mobility (AAM) is expected to organize unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) traffic into corridors at multiple altitudes. In this paper, we study the downlink (DL) and uplink (UL) capacity of a multi-layer Manhattan-grid corridor mesh served by a terrestrial fifth-generation (5G) new radio (NR) macro network. The corridor spacing and the numbers of layers, UAVs, and base stations are configurable. We combine the 3GPP aerial channel and antenna models, correlated UAV mobility, and frequency-selective fading with an NR physical-layer abstraction that includes channel aging and link adaptation. Results show that UAVs above 90 m experience a DL signal-to-interference-plus-noise ratio (SINR) about 17 dB below that of ground users, and that a dense macro network with $10^\circ$ downtilt leaves 17-29% of corridor positions without DL service under full-buffer load, regardless of corridor spacing. On a common layout, the carrier frequency (700 MHz, 3.5 GHz, or 7.2 GHz) changes the UAV SINR by less than 0.5 dB, since the corridor links are strongly interference-limited. The UL is the bottleneck: at 85% satisfaction, a 20 MHz carrier supports only about 3.4-4.1 UAVs/km$^2$ with 4 Mb/s of UL video per UAV.

title: Geometry-Aware Score-Repellent Monte Carlo
authors: Jie Hu, Lingyun Chen, Do Young Eun
abstract: The recently proposed Score-Repellent Monte Carlo (SRMC) method improves MCMC sampling by tilting the target density $π$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with the factor $\exp(-α\,θ_n^\top s(x))$, where the score function $s(x) = \nabla_x \log π(x)$, and $θ_n$ is the score average from past samples. However, a single scalar repellence strength $α\ge0$ cannot handle both the steep and the flat directions in anisotropic energy landscapes at once. We introduce \emph{Geometry-Aware SRMC} (GA-SRMC), which generalizes the Euclidean alignment to $θ^\top M s(x)$ for any symmetric positive-definite matrix $M$. A stochastic-approximation central limit theorem under a trace constraint on $M$ identifies the trace-normalized inverse Fisher $M_{\rm opt}\propto S^{-1}$ as the unique minimizer of the worst-direction covariance bound, elevating the Fisher information $S=\text{Cov}_π(s,s)$ from a proposal-side preconditioner (e.g., FisherMALA, natural gradient) to the bound-optimal repulsion-side matrix, with a single online estimate $\widehat S_n$ serving both roles at no additional computational cost. The full-Fisher online metric $M_n$ converges almost surely to $M_{\rm opt}$ and satisfies a CLT, providing a theoretical guarantee for the online implementation of the GA-SRMC framework. On an $8$-target simulation spanning the condition number $κ\in[1.3,100]$ and dimension $d\in[2,785]$, GA-SRMC dominates SRMC in ESS by $\boldsymbol{4.3\times}$ on anisotropic Gaussian ($κ=100$) and $\boldsymbol{6.8\times}$ on MNIST under the MALA baseline, by $\boldsymbol{16\text{--}32\%}$ on three well-conditioned logistic-regression posteriors, and by up to $\boldsymbol{+48\%}$ under FisherMALA; gains peak on the most anisotropic targets, and posterior-mean MSE is lower than with SRMC in all $16$ full-Fisher implementations.

title: Reweighting for Transfer Classification: Exact Risk Conversion and Minimax Adaptation
authors: Aoran Chen, Yang Feng
abstract: A source can make a training mixture easier to learn while making its accuracy less valuable for the target. We study how the training problem a source creates and the finite-sample error of learning it jointly determine target-risk guarantees under reweighting. For binary classification, for each pair of laws and each positive target weight, we derive the sharpest target excess hinge-risk bound implied by mixture excess alone, uniformly over clipped predictors. This exact conversion curve is determined by density-weighted local votes. A two-sample oracle inequality for weighted support vector machines supplies the mixture excess, and the composition becomes explicit for Gaussian kernels. On a tilted-boundary class, we establish the all-procedure minimax classification rate $[n+s_+^2/(m^{-1}+τ^2)]^{-1}$ in the transferable strength $s_+$ and the tilt $τ$, separating source sampling uncertainty ($m^{-1}$) from relation uncertainty ($τ^2$). A target-checked Gaussian-SVM selector adapts to unknown $s_+$ and $τ$ up to a logarithmic factor for fixed dimension, and retains the target-only rate up to the same factor against arbitrary independent sources under the stated target model. On a separate smooth opposition class, the minimax risk within the family of exact Gaussian SVMs fitted to the original labels with nonnegative weights is exponentially larger than the unrestricted minimax risk whenever the target sample is at most half the source sample, despite arbitrary data-dependent weighting and tuning. The value of a source thus depends on the training problem it creates, on what accuracy there means for the target, and on whether the permitted use of the source can implement the needed correction.
comment: 87 pages, 5 figures. Main text (32 pages) followed by the Supplementary Material

title: Semantic Extraction Framework for Goal-Oriented V2X Communication Supporting Safe Intersection Passage
authors: Haoran Yang, Shan Lu, Takaya Yamazato
abstract: This paper proposes a transmitter-side semantic extraction framework for goal-oriented Vehicle-to-Everything (V2X) communication supporting safe intersection passage. Instead of transmitting raw sensory data, roadside infrastructure extracts task-relevant semantic information from video and traffic-signal sequences and organizes them into compact semantic packets for low-latency driving-decision assistance. The intersection-passing problem is formulated as a set of traffic tasks under Japanese traffic regulations, and the proposed pipeline generates perception and intent semantics through object detection, object tracking, region-of-interest (ROI)-based semantic extraction, and recommended-action generation. The framework is implemented and evaluated on a self-constructed, CARLA-based single-vehicle dataset collected under clear weather conditions. Experimental results show high recommended-action accuracy within the tested task set, while the mean processing latency remains below the frame interval of the 15~fps input video.
comment: Accept by 2026 Asia-Pacific Conference on Communications

title: Real-Time Nonlinear Mixed-Integer Model Predictive Control With Horizon-Tail Relaxations
authors: Armin Nurkanović
abstract: Model predictive control (MPC) of nonlinear systems with discrete decisions leads to mixed-integer nonlinear programs (MINLPs) whose combinatorial complexity often prevents real-time deployment. In this paper, we propose a decomposition-based MPC method that reorders and reduces computations to shorten the delay between receiving a state measurement and applying the control input. Before the measurement arrives, we solve a continuous relaxation of the MINLP at a predicted state and construct a mixed-integer quadratic program (MIQP). Once the measured state is available, we solve the MIQP that reconstructs the discrete controls and simultaneously performs one sequential quadratic programming step toward the corresponding nonlinear solution. To reduce the combinatorial complexity in the horizon length, we either fix the integer controls or relax their integrality over the prediction horizon tail, while retaining an integer-feasible first control input. We derive error bounds relating the nonlinear objective values obtained with the horizon-tail approximations to the optimal value of the original mixed-integer problem. In a data center cooling example, the proposed method reduces mean feedback computation time by 94% relative to a state-of-the-art MINLP method with a total closed-loop cost difference of less than 1%.

title: GTCRN-SS: Lightweight Causal Speech Separation with Residual Allocation and Reconstruction Refinement
authors: Shao-Chun Hu, Zi-Xiang Lin, Hsin-Min Wang, Jeih-Weih Hung, Hung-Shin Lee
abstract: Low-complexity causal speech separation must preserve speaker information and allocate residual mixture energy without relying on future feature frames. We present GTCRN-SS, a two-stage time-frequency separator that adapts the compact GTCRN enhancement backbone to fixed-output speech separation. The model combines internal residual allocation, reconstruction-conditioned refinement, and frame-aligned recurrent-state transfer. Its complex-mask estimator assigns non-target content to an unreturned residual branch, while the complementary speech estimate conditions a second stage whose final masks remain anchored to the original mixture. A lightweight low-rank adapter transfers causal recurrent evidence between recursive executions without adding another recurrent memory network. The neural graph excludes future feature frames and incurs only the fixed analysis look-ahead of the centered short-time Fourier transform. On noisy Libri2Mix, GTCRN-SS achieves 10.1 dB SDRi and 9.5 dB SI-SNRi with fewer than one million parameters and a low computational footprint. Independently trained ablations confirm the benefits of recurrent-state transfer and reconstruction conditioning, and corpus-level diagnostics show that the internal branch primarily captures residual rather than target-speech content. These results establish GTCRN-SS as an effective quality-efficiency operating point for causal monaural speech separation.

title: TwinLight: A Multi-Timescale Physical-Layer-Aware T-API-Compliant Optical Domain Controller Digital Twin
authors: Carlos Natalino, Piotr Lechowicz, Renato Ambrosone, Enrico Miotto, Vittorio Curri, Paolo Monti
abstract: We demonstrate TwinLight, an open-source optical-network digital twin acting as an optical domain controller. Its T-API REST and telemetry streaming interfaces expose a physical-layer engine that combines a GNPy steady-state baseline with four analytical transients.
comment: Demonstration presented at ECOC 2026, Málaga, Spain, Sept. 2026. Paper ID Tu2-Ex1/1440. Code in https://github.com/carlosnatalino/TwinLight

title: Data-driven representation of continuous-time linear time-invariant behaviors via Hankel integral operators
authors: Fritz A. Engeln, Marta Zagórowska, Jan-Willem van Wingerden
abstract: We present a data-driven representation of the finite-horizon behavior of deterministic controllable continuous-time LTI systems. We first introduce a notion of persistency of excitation for continuous-time signals that does not require the signal to be differentiable. We then show that, when the input is persistently exciting in this sense, the closure of the range of a Hankel integral operator built from a single input-output trajectory equals the behavior of the system over a finite time horizon. This result provides a nonparametric representation of system trajectories directly in terms of measured data, without requiring an explicit parametric model of the system.

title: Artificial Shoppers and Attention Competition
authors: Xiaomeng Guo, Fasheng Xu, Xiaoli Zhang
abstract: We study how AI shopping interfaces affect price competition, platform profit, and consumer welfare. A platform hosts two of three products of different quality. Without AI, consumers compare the hosted pair under salience distortion and overweight whichever attribute, price or quality, stands out. Under assistance, an AI assistant recommends the two products with the highest true utility, leaving consumers to make the same distorted comparison. Under delegation, an AI agent selects the best product, subject to purchase approval. Both modes access all products and know consumers' preferences; firms price strategically. First, assistance can soften competition despite expanded product access. The middle-quality firm may forgo low-valuation consumers because attracting them requires cutting the price paid by higher-valuation consumers as well. Relative to no AI with the same assortment, assistance lowers both hosted prices under the high- and low-quality pair but can raise both under the high- and middle-quality pair. Second, we identify an alignment paradox: some consumers can become worse off than without AI even though their best option remains recommended and becomes cheaper. Salience can induce a switch to a lower-quality product whose quality loss exceeds the saving relative to the original purchase. The assistant ranks products accurately but does not optimize the shortlist for consumers' realized welfare. Third, assistance can raise both platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus with the high- and middle-quality pair; delegation can do so with the high- and low-quality pair. Fourth, among AI designs, the platform weakly prefers delegation with the high- and middle-quality pair wherever all compared pricing equilibria exist. Yet this preferred design can yield lower platform profit and aggregate consumer surplus than the no-AI optimum.

title: SmartBloch-Agent: An Agentic Framework for Automated MRI Sequence Design and Optimization
authors: Jiakai Yang, Haoye Zheng, Yixiao Yue, Qinqin Yang, Zhong Chen, Shuhui Cai, Congbo Cai
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) pulse sequences organize radiofrequency excitation, gradient encoding, and signal acquisition, determining magnetization evolution and image formation. Sequence research requires translating imaging objectives into executable protocols meeting physical and acquisition constraints, refined via physical simulation, signal reconstruction, and scientific evaluation. Sequence construction, physical verification, parameter search, and assessment involve many tools and manual decisions, limiting automation from objective to verifiable sequence. We develop SmartBloch-Agent, an integrated framework for automated MRI sequence design and optimization. Given objectives and scientific constraints in natural language, an AI agent interprets goals, plans tasks, orchestrates tools, and makes feedback-informed decisions, drawing on a construction module and optimizers for structural design and parameter search. Our GPU-accelerated SmartBloch engine supplies physical computation for both stages, so the framework configures, per sequence and objective, event validation, Full-Bloch magnetization evolution, signal acquisition, image reconstruction, and scientific evaluation, and closes the loop without external MRI simulators. Results return to the agent to guide sequence revision, parameter optimization, and candidate selection, and the design files carry simulation, reconstruction, and evaluation evidence, forming an output package for a real-scanner workflow. Experiments show the framework automatically designs and optimizes MRI sequences for varied objectives and constraints, refines candidates with physical feedback, and improves several parameter-estimation metrics and downstream quantitative reconstruction. SmartBloch-Agent unifies objectives, design, physical execution, and evaluation into a continuous workflow for end-to-end automation of MRI sequence research.

title: Graph representations of dislocation networks
authors: Gaurav Lathiya, Markus Stricker
abstract: The mechanical response of a crystal is governed by the evolving network of dislocations it contains, yet quantitatively linking the `state of that network' to its yield stress remains challenging. Here we represent the dislocation networks obtained from discrete dislocation dynamic simulation as graphs, using five distinct graph representations, characterize each network through a compact set of topological properties, and predict the yield stress from these graph properties and the applied strain rate using a standard random forest model evaluated with strain rate stratified cross-validation. The model predicts the yield stress with $R^2\approx0.86-0.90$ across all box sizes and $R^2\approx0.91-0.94$ for larger box sizes, and this accuracy is consistent across all five representations, indicating that the topology-stress relationship is a robust feature of the graph properties rather than an artefact of any single graph representation. We propose graph topology as a compact and robust route for connecting the microstructural state of a dislocation network to its mechanical response in addition to established variables.

title: Scalable BLE Channel Sounding Localization with Ranging-Assisted PDoA
authors: Jorg Wieme, Eli De Poorter, Jeroen Hoebeke
abstract: Bluetooth Channel Sounding (CS) enables accurate phase-based ranging, but multi-anchor localization requires sequential ranging exchanges that limit scalability and increase measurement latency. This paper proposes Ranging-Assisted Phase Difference of Arrival (RA-PDoA), a scalable BLE localization architecture combining one active anchor performing a standard two-way CS exchange with multiple passive receive-only anchors observing the same transmissions. A channel-recovery framework is derived that enables passive anchors to reconstruct a channel response suitable for super-resolution delay estimation, allowing multipath-robust ranging without participating in a two-way exchange. Coarse arrival-time information is further used to bound the position estimate and reject inconsistent range solutions. A comprehensive evaluation characterizes the impact of multipath propagation, body shadowing, synchronization requirements, oscillator impairments, anchor placement, and deployment inaccuracies, thereby quantifying the practical infrastructure requirements for scalable BLE localization. Simulation results in modeled indoor environments show that RA-PDoA reduces the 90th-percentile localization error from 175.3 cm to 95.5 cm under body shadowing while maintaining an airtime requirement independent of the number of anchors. The results demonstrate that a single active ranging link enables scalable and multipath-robust BLE Channel Sounding localization.
comment: 14 pages, 5 figures, 7 tables, Appendix, For reproducibility code available at https://gitlab.ilabt.imec.be/iwine/ra-pdoa-simulator

title: TurtLES: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Turbulent 3D Neural PDE Surrogates
authors: Jarno Platenburg, Armand Kassaï Koupaï, Paola Cinnella, Patrick Gallinari
abstract: Machine-learning surrogates are increasingly used to accelerate computational fluid dynamics, yet progress is limited by the lack of benchmarks capturing realistic, time-dependent turbulent flows. We introduce TurtLES, a 14 TB dataset of 3D turbulent cylinder wakes in the shear-layer transition regime, computed via high-fidelity implicit large-eddy simulations. The dataset contains 400 trajectories of 400 time steps each, with 3-11 million points per frame, spanning variations in geometry, Reynolds number, and angle of attack. Unlike existing datasets, TurtLES combines (i) physically realistic turbulence with an active energy cascade driven by vortex stretching, (ii) dense irregular meshes, and (iii) long-horizon temporal dynamics. We benchmark state-of-the-art neural operators on autoregressive rollouts and identify key failure modes, including temporal instability, loss of small-scale energy, and challenges in learning on large irregular domains. TurtLES provides a new benchmark for evaluating surrogate models on 3D turbulent wakes at industrially relevant mesh resolution.

title: Kernel-Based Learning of Analytic Operators and Parametric PDEs
authors: Giovanni S. Alberti, Markus Holzleitner, Lorenzo Rosasco, Matteo Santacesaria
abstract: We study kernel-based learning of analytic operators from finite samples, with a focus on how the regularity of the target should determine the choice of the kernel. We establish embeddings of analytic operators into vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and derive finite-sample, high-probability guarantees that quantify the uncertainty due to random sampling: in the noiseless setting, suitable analytic kernels yield rates exponential in a fractional power of the sample size, while Sobolev-type kernels yield polynomial rates. We apply the theory to the solution operator of a parametric elliptic PDE, where the training data are themselves finite-element approximations, and obtain bounds that separate the sampling and discretization contributions to the error and prescribe how the mesh size should be coupled to the sample size. The results are illustrated numerically.

title: Locally Adaptive Conformal Prediction for Polynomial Chaos Expansions
authors: Dimitrios Loukrezis, Arthur Hatstatt, Bruno Sudret, Dimitris G. Giovanis
abstract: This work develops a locally adaptive jackknife+ conformal prediction framework for polynomial chaos expansions. Therein, the non-conformity scores are normalized with an auxiliary polynomial chaos expansion trained on the log-transformed leave-one-out residuals of the base model. We show that the coverage guarantee of jackknife+ conformal prediction carries over to the adaptive intervals if the leave-one-out auxiliary models are trained on nested leave-one-out residuals. For fixed-basis polynomial chaos expansions fitted by ordinary least squares, all required quantities are derived in closed form and the guarantee-preserving adaptive intervals are obtained from a single model fit, without any model retraining. For sparse polynomial chaos expansions, where multiple model fits are necessary, we propose a heuristic simplification that limits the computational overhead of adaptivity at the cost of the formal coverage guarantee. Numerical experiments on an academic benchmark with known heteroscedastic noise and on an engineering simulation dataset show that the suggested method attains the target coverage while providing intervals that adapt to local prediction uncertainty, therefore being considerably more statistically efficient. These advantages are particularly prominent in high-uncertainty regions of the input space, where the performance of non-adaptive methods degrades substantially.

title: Half-precision inference of AI weather prediction models: negligible loss of skill at a fraction of the cost
authors: Stefan Siegert
abstract: AI weather prediction models are released with 32-bit (fp32) weights and run in fp32 by default, although current GPUs compute much faster in 16-bit formats. We run five publicly available models -- Aurora, Pangu-Weather, FourCastNet, SFNO and FastNet -- on a single 16 GB GPU from 52 initial dates in 2024, in fp32 and with their networks in half precision (fp16), and verify the forecasts against ERA5. The physical state must stay in fp32: converting the whole model rounds it in physical units, which in fp16 overflows and in bf16 discards meaningful information. With the state, its normalisation and denormalisation in fp32, running the network in fp16 changes the global RMSE by at most 1.4%, and by about 0.5% or less for four of the five models, equivalent to less than one hour of lead time up to day 8 and at most two hours at day 10. The differences show no systematic pattern by region, scale or for tropical and extratropical storms, apart from a small tropical penalty in FourCastNet, and fp16 leaves the CRPS, spread and calibration of Aurora's ensemble almost unchanged. No value overflowed fp16's numeric range (+/-65,504); the largest stay 38 to 544 times below it. A 10-day forecast in fp16 is 1.3-3.5 times faster than in fp32 and uses 1.4-3.7 times less energy. Sensitivity experiments show that rules of thumb from other applications of reduced precision carry over only partly: the first and last layers dominate for some models but not for others, and no type of layer is sensitive on its own. For running AI weather models on a single GPU, fp16 with the state in fp32 is practically lossless at a fraction of the cost. bf16, often preferred for its wider range, is as fast but less accurate than fp16 for every model, and simple 8-bit quantisation costs far more skill.

title: Quantum Integration Software Suite For HPC-Quantum Computing Workflows
authors: Mateusz Meller, Joseph C. R. Thacker, Thomas W. Keal, Vendel Szeremi
abstract: In this work, we focus on addressing challenges related to modelling the integration of conventional high-performance computing (HPC) and quantum computing (QC). We introduce the Quantum Assembly Compiler (QASC) for OpenQASM3.0 files. The compiler produces an executable that leverages the high-performance simulator QuEST to simulate quantum programs. Additionally, we introduce a performance modelling tool, QACC-perf, which can estimate the cost of integrating QC in classical HPC workflows, as well as the execution time of the quantum circuits. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of these tools in the context of multiscale quantum chemistry workflows using the ChemShell computational chemistry environment.

title: New persistent chain spaces: identifying and computing the relevant persistent Laplacians of a filtration
authors: Joris Kirchner, Martina Vittorietti
abstract: Persistent homology (PH) summarizes the topological features of data that persist across scales, but it is insensitive to many geometric properties. Persistent Laplacians (PLs) address this limitation: for a pair of simplicial complexes in a filtration, the kernel of the persistent Laplacian recovers the persistent Betti number, while its non-zero spectrum carries additional geometric information. However, PLs are defined for individual pairs of filtration values, so analysing a whole filtration requires evaluating many operators that largely contain the same information, and the result is hard to summarize and interpret. In this paper, we show that this redundancy has a precise structure. For each pair of filtration values, we decompose the space of chains underlying the persistent up-Laplacian into the contributions inherited from the neighboring pairs and a remaining part, which we call the new persistent chain space. We show that the new persistent chain spaces of all earlier pairs form a direct sum decomposition of this space, so that every persistent up-Laplacian in the filtration is determined by them. Moreover, the new persistent chain spaces are non-trivial only at pairs given by the persistence pairing in the same and in the next homological dimension, so that the persistence pairing determines exactly where the persistent up-Laplacian can change. Experiments on several types of point clouds show that evaluating persistent Laplacians only at these pairs reduces the computation time, both for our implementation and for existing software.

title: Beyond Feasibility: Efficient and Robust On-Device Localization with UWB Concurrent Transmissions
authors: Enrico Soprana, Michael Stocker, Davide Vecchia, Matteo Trobinger, Carlo Alberto Boano, Gian Pietro Picco
